quotes.quote: The Kutch Bandhani is an ancient, dyeing technique, wherein the fabric is tied in intricate patterns with the help of nails, beads or grain, which prevents the colour from seeping into the tied areas during dyeing.

Bandhani (Figure 1) is the traditional craft of tie-dye whereby patterning on textiles is created by tightly tying multiple parts of the fabric with thread to resist dyes and create dot like puckered designs.
bandhani work (a dyeing technique in which patterns are formed from arrangements of resist-dyed dots)
A tie-dyeing technique used to make patterned fabrics, Bandhani in its many variations is identified by light circular or square-shaped repeating motifs on a dark ground.
The ter bandhani is derived from the Sanskrit verbal root bandh ("to bind, to tie").
It derives its name from the Sanskrit word baandh, meaning "to tie,"
Bandhani is an expression used in Gujarat for textiles where different designs are produced by tying individual parts of the fabric before dyeing.

Bandhani, is the name given to the characteristic feature on Indian tie and dye. It refers to the little dot created in the centre of square or circle motifs as the dye seeps into the fabric material.
The manufacturing process of Kutch Bandhani products of Gujarat, using tie-dye method on the woven fabric, is unique with intricate designs and Rai Dana (Mustard Seed) dots.
The manufacturing process is so cumber-some and time consuming to make a final product. The entire manufacturing process is manual.
The Geographical Area of production of Kutch Bandhani is Kutch district of Gujarat

Bandhani is mainly produced in Gujarat. All the artisan of the bandhani are mostly immigrants form Sindh before Independence.

It is believed that the tie & dye technique was introduced some centuries back by a fakir from Sindh. However there is no historical reference about the exact time or period.
The bandhani technique was originally practised by the Khatri community in Sindh and subsequently gained popularity among artisans of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh.
Experts believe the technique was brought to Kutch by Khatri craftsmen from Sindh, probably in the 16th century.
It is believed that this craft exists from a very long time say about from 6th century.

Our earliest evidence of the use of Kutch Bandhani cloth in India is in the depiction on the walls of Ajanta caves, which dates back to 6th century AD. Here, women are shown wearing blouses with clearly discernible simple dotted tie-dye patterns.
Other earliest references to "Kutch Bandhani" fabrics is in Bana"s Harshacharita life of King Harsh (606-648 A.D.)
the poet writes that at the wedding of one of the prince"s sister "old matrons were skilled in many sorts of (textile) pattern-ship, some of which were in the process of being tied (Bandhyamana).

Literature references in the 14th century include the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, who described that a single piece silk cloth which was dyed in 5 colours being sent to the Emperor of China from Muhammad Tughlug"s court. This piece may indicate Kutch Bandhani cloth.
Another Gujarat text of the 15th century confirms that Mandvi in Kutch was renowned for its dyeing odhanis even then and in the second quarter of the 16th century.
Mandvi in Kutch was renowned for its dyeing odhanis even then and in the second quarter of the 16th century. It is still an important tie & dye centre. (Murphy, Veronica-1991)

The "Bandhani" type of fabrics of Indian origin found at fostat in Egapt and attributed to the late medieval period (Irwin and Hall, l97I:17 and Plate 5A) appeared to have been only cheap imitations of true "Bandhani" and made with printing blocks.

From the 12th century onwards, Jain script painting from Western India illustrates many garments with dotted pattern, which seems to be tie and dye. Several of them are with the Tribundi pattern (group of three dots) popular in Gujarat up to the 20th century.
True Gujarat Bandhani is mentioned in Varnaka, the seventeenth century inventory under bandhalaya (Moti Chandra, 1961:24).

The designs are marked out on a thick plastic sheet. Pinholes are made around the pattern. The "printing ink" is a mixture of "geru" and black colour or soot mixed with water. The "ink" seeps through the holes to print the pattern on the cloth.
While the blocks are the traditional printing tools, most dyers today apply the geru with stencils made of plastic Farma paper.
Traditionally, blocks were used to print the designs, but craftspeople now use stencils made of farma paper, a type of laminated paper.
Traditionally, wooden blocks dipped in "geru" (red oxide mixed with water) were used to print the design, but now, plastic farma paper is used.
The cloth which is bleached, usually thin cotton, silk or wool is folded two times and a design are marked out in the form of dots.
The printing paste is that of direct dyes and can be washable. This printing is done for making designs for tying work.
The cloth is folded into four or more layers for tying. The "rangara" (colourer) marks the lay-out of the pattern with special geru (a burntsienna mixed with water) on the material.

The Gujarati craftsman prefers to work without any aids like finger nail, small metal ring etc. The reason behind is, the flow is much better when working with bare hands and there is no risk of damaging the cloth.
Bandhani is a type of tie-dye textile decorated by plucking the cloth with the fingernails into many tiny bindings that form a figurative design.
As per the printed pattern, tiny sections of cloth are pinched by hand, or raised with a metal ring, and bound with a strong thread - traditionally by women known as bandhanaras.
who raises and pinches the fabric in the marked designs using a pointed small fingernail or metal ring with a pointed tip.
The time taken for tying work varies from 4 to 90 days depending upon the Kutch Bandhani design.
One of the important specialties of the Bandhani is that a meter long of cloth can have millions of tiny knots known as "Bheendi" in the local Kutch language.
A metre length of cloth can have thousands of tiny knots known as 'Bheendi' in the local language.
There are two different styles of Kutch Bandhani. One has the popular dots and the other has lines called "Laheria". "Laheria" originates from the "lahar" which means waves.
It is tied in a similar design of thin lines gradually flowing into thicker lines. The tying process is usually done on bleached white cloth or cloth which is dyed yellow.
The cloth is rolled and tied with a thick thread which is wound at an interval of about an inch. The thread is wound on a long stick, which enables them to tie thread tightly on the cloth.
The thread is wound on a long stick, which enables them to tie thread tightly on the cloth. This work is mainly carried out by women and girls.
After the tying process, tied cloth is taken for dyeing. It is bleached First, and then rinsed in several tubs of water. Then it is dyed in another colour.
The desired amount of chemicals are put in a piece of cloth and swirled in hot water, then the cloth is put in the water and swirled around with the help of wooden stick.
After the desired shade is achieved it is removed and rinsed in several tubs of water. The process continues till the desired colour combination is achieved.
This process may be repeated multiple times for each colour included in the pattern, starting with the lightest shade.
The dyer always starts with the lightest colour (usually yellow), sends the fabric to be tied again if needed, and repeats the process until all the desired colours have been added.
If there are two colours, the pattern is tied again after the first dye, and then dyed again.

Colouring of the border involves another technique. The tied cloth is gathered and tightly wrapped in plastic, and wound over tightly by a rubber strip. The dye is manually scrubbed into the material taking care that wrapped areas does not come into contact with the dye.
Vat and Naphtha dyes are used for cotton and Acid dyes are used for silk clothes.
Earlier, most Kutch Bandhani cloth was maroon colour of alizarin derived from madder and black or brown derived from various plants which are very expensive.
The process using vegetable dyes requires more time and more use of water.
Bright colours are expensive and difficult to produce but synthetic dyes are affordable.
The colours used in the process are natural and hence best colour combinations are possible.
Chemical colours are never used directly, as some crystals could get caught in the material and may damage the material.

With the discovery of fast dyes which can also be applied cold, it has become possible to dye individual parts by hand with piece of felt which is tied round a wooden handle, with which the dye can be applied.

The large odhanis have similar patterns, with large central medallions against a black ground, which give them the name chandrokhani or 'moon-like'.
The basic motifs used in Chandrokani are - in the center there is a big circular motif called gul and in the borders a wavy line called - Nag ni Sar or Sarpvel which means snake boarder.
Earlier Chandrokhani was in red dots with black ground, and red pallu (Border) with golden zari, but now other colours are also used.

Other traditional Bandhani include the Bavanbagh (the 52 gardens) and the Rasamandali (associated with Raas, the traditional dance form of Gujarat), both of which have patterned red backgrounds teamed with contrasting borders
Other traditional bandhani designs from Gujarat include the bavanbagh and the rasamandali, in which motifs such as mango trees, peacocks and elephants are also prevalent.

Ambadaal means mango branches. In this design motifs like mango leaves and branches, along with elephants and statue of woman carrying water pot are also used. The mango tree is the symbol of fertility, elephant signifies wealth, woman carrying water pot signifies auspiciousness.
Bar-bhag means twelve parts. It is a pattern formed by diagonal checks in the ground and each rhombus has a motif of ritual symbolism.

Veerbut (Veer Bhet Bhat): It is a brother's gift to sister on the occasion of Raksha Bandhan. This traditional design sari is always in deep green colour which signifies growth, prosperity and fertility.
A Gharchola is a saree woven with gold or silver zari thread and embellished with Bandhani that a man gives his bride, and the tie-dyed veil worn by the bride is known as a Chunri.
The Bandhani saree, one of many tie and dye garments is a symbol of married life for many women. It is regarded as an article of great splendour that promises the bride a good future.

the social, economic and cultural connotations of a particular Bandhani is determined by the base fabric (gajji silk, fine cotton, muslin or wool), the design and its associations with festivals and rites of passage such as marriages and death.
The quality of the craftsmanship can be judged by the contours or kaff of the dots formed, as well as by the uniformity of their size and spacing.

Traditional bandhani designs are valued based on the execution of this technique - patterns with numerous small and closely spaced dots are preferred to those with fewer, widely spaced or irregular dots.

The entire cloth is then dipped in boiling dye for several minutes, washed and left to sun-dry. The small quantities of dye in the tied portions leak away while the concentrated dye in the surrounding cloth remains.

The process continues till the desired colour combination is achieved. The cloth is then dried without opening the folds. It must be dried thoroughly; as the cloth could get damaged if opened when it is still damp as the air pockets may have been trapped inside the knots.
After it is dried, the folds of the cloth are pulled apart in a particular way, thus releasing the knots and revealing the patterns.
For opening it, the Kutch Bandhani material is pulled crosswise forcibly, so that, simultaneously, all the ties open up and the tie-threads lie on the material in a loose mass.
is done when two ends of the material are pulled crosswise tightly, loosening and opening the ties to reveal the colours and patterns in the fabric.
